display.purpose: The product name on the start card. The loudest word on the screen.

headline.purpose: The four stat figures. Deliberately sized under Display — the numbers argue, the name wins.

title.purpose: Landing section headings; the single size the landing prose added to the card scale.

cta.purpose: The start button, and the document base size.

body.purpose: Prose, gesture rows, the walkthrough prompt.

ui.purpose: Settings rows, labels, selects, section names.

detail.purpose: Hints, sub-lines, fine print, readouts beside a control.

label.purpose: Uppercase group headings, stat labels, hand names, rail tips.

readout.purpose: Tabular values that change live: knob values, octaves, tab numbers, frame rate.

micro.purpose: The smallest readouts the product allows: pad numerals, the filter kind, an effect row value, a stepper arrow.

shadows.name: fader-glow
shadows.purpose: The only box-shadow in the system, and it is a meter rather than elevation: both radius and alpha are driven by --level, the measured audio, so a lit fader segment keeps ringing through the release and the reverb tail.

surfaces.name: glass
surfaces.value: background: rgba(18, 22, 32, 0.92); backdrop-filter: blur(10px); border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1)
surfaces.purpose: Anything floating over the camera feed: HUD bar, walkthrough card, Stop button, rail tooltip. The blur is legibility over moving video, not decoration.

surfaces.name: tone-console
surfaces.purpose: The settings column and the rail, sharing one ground so an open panel and its rail read as a single surface.

surfaces.name: tone-recessed
surfaces.purpose: Cards inside the panel: chord slots, effect rows, figure frames.

surfaces.name: tone-raised
surfaces.purpose: Controls sitting on those cards: selects, inputs, tabs, steppers, rail buttons, knob bodies.

motion.name: pad-attack
motion.purpose: A chord pad lighting on strike. Matches the note committing.

motion.name: pad-release
motion.purpose: A chord pad letting go. Matches the note releasing — the asymmetry is what makes the bar feel played rather than refreshed.

motion.name: meter
motion.purpose: Fader segments tracking measured level. Linear because it is a meter.

motion.name: reveal
motion.purpose: Rail tooltip fade on hover and focus-visible.

motion.name: zone-dim
motion.purpose: A HUD half dimming back when its hand leaves the frame.

motion.name: panel-slide
motion.purpose: The settings panel opening: margin-right on desktop, translateY on the mobile bottom sheet.

motion.name: reduced-motion
motion.purpose: Under prefers-reduced-motion the HUD zone, pads and fader segments drop their transitions entirely and snap. Values stay readable; nothing merely slows down.

tints.name: left-edge / right-edge
tints.purpose: A border saying which hand a thing belongs to.

tints.name: left-legend / right-legend
tints.purpose: A ground under something that labels a hand: the start card columns, a gesture badge, the filter graph span.

tints.name: left-live / right-live
tints.purpose: A ground under something playing, selected or running right now: a struck pad, the active section tab, the selected waveform.

tints.name: accent-live
tints.purpose: The same 12%, for the rail button, which belongs to the app rather than to either hand.

browserSurfaces.name: selection
browserSurfaces.purpose: The accent, not a hand colour — a selection is the interface acting, not a hand playing.

browserSurfaces.name: focus-ring
browserSurfaces.value: :is(button, a, input, select, [tabindex]):focus { outline: none; } :is(button, a, input, select, [tabindex]):focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
browserSurfaces.purpose: One ordered pair covering every control in the product. Equal specificity, so the later focus-visible rule wins whenever it matches; a pointer press never leaves a ring behind.

browserSurfaces.name: focus-ring-on-fill
browserSurfaces.purpose: The exception: a control already filled with the accent cannot ring in the accent. Against the card showing through the 2px offset gap an accent ring reads 5.88:1 and looks like a halo; Screen White reads 15.26:1 and looks like an edge.

browserSurfaces.name: scrollbar
browserSurfaces.value: .start-screen only: scrollbar-width: thin; scrollbar-color: var(--border-hover) transparent; with a ::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb pill inset by a 3px transparent border clipped to the padding box
browserSurfaces.purpose: Deliberately not applied to .settings-body, the other scroll container: styling a scrollbar opts the container out of the macOS overlay bar, and the 10px it then takes comes out of the 340px panel.

browserSurfaces.name: native-tint
browserSurfaces.purpose: Inherited, so range thumbs and checkboxes take Periwinkle without a rule each.

layout.name: panel-width
layout.purpose: The settings column. Every grid inside it is solved against the 282px a row leaves.

layout.name: rail-width
layout.purpose: Reserved as padding-right on the app shell rather than given to a flex item, because both the rail and the panel are positioned rather than laid out.

layout.name: panel-overlay
layout.value: position: absolute; right: 56px; transform: translateX(100%) when closed
layout.purpose: The panel slides over the camera rather than squeezing it: one compositor transform instead of 200ms of relaying the video, canvas and HUD, and the stage holding still is why the view of your hands does not jump. The HUD shifts 170px and Stop 340px to clear it — exactly where a shrinking stage used to put them.

layout.name: slot-indent
layout.purpose: Slot badge (24px) plus its gap (10px). Lines two and three of a chord slot indent to it so they align without a container.

layout.name: reading-column
layout.purpose: The start card and the landing prose share one column so they align flush.

components.name: Primary Button

components.css: .ds-hud { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 18px; padding: 10px 18px; border-radius: 16px; border: 1px solid var(--border, rgba(255,255,255,0.1)); background: rgba(18,22,32,0.92); backdrop-filter: blur(10px); font-family: ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif; color: var(--text, #e8ecf4); width: max-content; --level: 0.7; } .ds-hud-zone { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; transition: opacity 0.2s ease; } .ds-hud-zone--idle { opacity: 0.45; } .ds-hud-chord { font-size: 14px; font-weight: 600; color: var(--left, #4dd6ff); } .ds-hud-section { align-self: stretch; display: flex; align-items: center; padding: 0 16px; border-left: 1px solid var(--border, rgba(255,255,255,0.1)); border-right: 1px solid var(--border, rgba(255,255,255,0.1)); font-size: 11px; letter-spacing: 0.08em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--muted, #8b93a7); } .ds-hud-kind { font-size: 10px; letter-spacing: 0.08em; color: var(--muted, #8b93a7); } .ds-hud-hz { font-size: 12px; min-width: 7ch; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; } .ds-fader { display: flex; gap: 3px; } .ds-seg { width: 5px; height: 14px; border-radius: 2px; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.12); transition: background-color 0.08s linear, box-shadow 0.08s linear; } .ds-seg--on { background: var(--right, #ff9f43); box-shadow: 0 0 calc(2px + var(--level, 0) * 8px) rgba(255,159,67, calc(0.3 + var(--level, 0) * 0.5)); } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .ds-hud-zone, .ds-seg { transition: none; } }

narrative.overview:
The room is dark and the player is lit. Everything that is not a hand recedes into graphite — five near-black grounds separated only by a few percent of lightness and a 10% white hairline — so that the two colours that matter have nothing to compete with. Cyan is the left hand. Amber is the right hand. That code is taught on the start card before the camera is even on, drawn onto the player's own knuckles by the overlay, played back by the chord pads, used to group the pickers in the settings panel, and stamped on every gesture badge in the reference. A player learns it once and it is never violated.

The character is precise but warm. The mechanics are instrument-grade: dials sweep 270° with the dead zone at the bottom, the hardware convention; every changing number is tabular and sits in a reserved width so nothing in the interface reflows because a value moved; a chord pad lights in 60ms and lets go in 240ms because that is what the note does. But the palette is warmer than a professional tool would permit itself — four envelope colours, a two-ended amber filter sweep, a seven-step green ramp for the rack — and the discipline is not in withholding colour, it is in never spending it on something that is not live.

There is no typeface to load and no image to fetch. The interface is the system sans stack, line art drawn in-repo from the same maths the audio runs on, and colour. That is the entire material vocabulary, and its restraint is why a translucent bar of controls can sit on top of a live camera feed without obscuring the person in it.
keyCharacteristics: Two hand colours carrying one meaning each, used identically in five places.
Grey at rest, colour when live — saturation is a state, not a style.
Five graphite grounds and a 10% hairline; no drop shadows anywhere.
Glass over the video, opaque tone in the column — two grounds, one rule.
Tabular numerals in reserved widths; the layout never moves because a number did.
Every glyph drawn in-repo from the audio’s own maths, stroked in currentColor.
System sans only. No web fonts, no icon packages, no raster UI assets.

rules.name: The Two Hands Rule
rules.body: Cyan is the left hand and amber is the right hand, everywhere, without exception. A hand colour on a control that belongs to the other hand — or to neither — is a defect, not a variation.

rules.name: The Live Colour Rule
rules.body: Grey is the resting state of everything. A colour appearing on screen means that thing is playing, selected, running, or being held. Colour is never spent on hierarchy, emphasis, or decoration. The tint names enforce this: a -legend ground labels, a -live ground means now, and reaching for the wrong one is visible in the diff.

rules.name: The Chain Ramp Rule
rules.body: The effects rack is one hue in six steps, lightest at the front of the signal path and darkest at the back. Reordering the chain reorders the shading. Anything that is not in the chain — the tempo — must leave the family.

rules.name: The Six Sizes Rule
rules.body: The start card runs on six sizes and no others: 32 title, 28 stat figure, 15 call to action, 14 prose, 12 detail, 11 uppercase label. Anything that lands between two of them is a mistake, not a nuance. New surfaces extend this scale only by adding a size deliberately and once — the landing prose added exactly one (20px) and reused everything else; the app chrome added 13 for settings rows and 10 for the smallest readouts. Nine sizes carry the entire product. A tenth needs a reason.

rules.name: The Reserved Width Rule
rules.body: Any number that changes gets tabular-nums and a reserved width. The filter readout holds 7ch because "2.4 kHz" is the widest it gets; the octave stepper holds 22px; the pad’s note line holds 15px of height whether or not a chord is sounding. Nothing in the interface may move because a value did.

rules.name: The 340 Rule
rules.body: The settings panel is 340px and every grid inside it is solved against the 282px that leaves. A control that only fits by shrinking the panel’s type is the wrong control.

rules.name: The 24px Floor Rule
rules.body: No control is smaller than 24x24, the WCAG 2.2 minimum target. The panel’s steppers and the tempo lock were 22x15, 22x20 and 16x16 — desktop-first sizes on a surface that becomes a touch-driven bottom sheet below 860px. Where a control must stay visually small, grow the target, not the ink.

rules.name: The Load-Bearing Width Rule
rules.body: Inside the panel, 10px is a feature. Styling a scrollbar — scrollbar-color, scrollbar-width, or any ::-webkit-scrollbar rule — opts that container out of the macOS overlay scrollbar and makes it take layout width. In .settings-body that costs the effect row’s flexible name column 60px to 51px, under what "Tremolo" needs. Theme a scrollbar only where the container’s width is not solved against.

rules.name: The Two Grounds Rule
rules.body: Anything floating over the camera is glass; anything in the settings column is opaque tone. Never mix them — a blurred card inside the panel or an opaque card over the video both break the model.

rules.name: The Only Shadow Rule
rules.body: The one box-shadow in the system is a meter, driven by real audio. A shadow used to lift a surface is a defect.

rules.name: The Round Means Reach Rule
rules.body: If it is a bare glyph you press without reading, it is round. If it carries a word or a number you read, it is a rectangle.

rules.name: The Hairline-Only Rule
rules.body: Every border in the system is the same 10% white hairline. Weight never varies; only colour and dash do, and only to signal state.

dos: Do bind every colour to a meaning before you use it. If you cannot say what a new colour is — which hand, which stage, which position in the chain — it does not belong in the palette.
Do give any changing number font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums and a reserved width, so the layout cannot move because a value did.
Do use the hairline (1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.1)) for every border, and change only its colour or dash to signal state.

Do let the global :focus / :focus-visible pair cover new controls rather than writing a focus rule per component; add a control to the selector list only if it is focusable by something other than a tag or tabindex.
Do theme any browser surface a new feature exposes — selection, caret, scrollbar, native control tint — from the palette, the first time it appears.
Do match glass to video and opaque tone to the column — the Two Grounds Rule.
Do draw new glyphs in-repo, stroked in currentColor, with round caps and joins, at the weight its size calls for (1.5 at 20px, 2 at picker size, 3 for figure curves).
Do solve any new panel layout against 282px of usable row width.
donts: Don’t use colour decoratively. Grey is the resting state of everything; a colour on screen means that thing is live, selected, or running. Colour is never spent on hierarchy or emphasis.

Don’t introduce an icon package, an icon font, or an imported SVG set. Every glyph in this product is drawn from the same maths the audio runs on — waveformPath, effectGlyphPaths, filterShape, adsrShape — which is why the picture and the sound can never disagree.

Don’t invent a second type scale. Six sizes carry the card (32/28/15/14/12/11) and the app chrome adds 20, 13 and 10 deliberately. A size that lands between two existing ones is a mistake, not a nuance.

Don’t animate anything that is not encoding audio. The pad’s 60ms/240ms asymmetry and the fader’s level-driven glow are the sound made visible; under prefers-reduced-motion values must snap, never merely slow down.
Don’t add a drop shadow. Depth is tone and glass; the only box-shadow in the system is a meter.
Don’t give a hand colour to something that is not that hand, and don’t give a hand colour to the app’s own chrome — that is Periwinkle’s job.
Don’t style the scrollbar of a container whose width something is solved against. It stops being an overlay bar and starts taking 10px.

Don’t put a thick coloured edge on one side of a card to signal what it belongs to. The system already has an idiom for that — a tinted border with a wash of the same colour — and it is used at 8% for a legend, 10–12% for a live state.
Don’t put Screen White or any near-white on a filled accent surface. It fails AA. Filled accent takes --on-accent.
Don’t load a web font or ship a raster UI asset. The interface is system sans, line art and colour, and its ability to render instantly from prerendered markup depends on staying that way.
